newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan says India creates dangerous environment.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan says India creates dangerous environment.

text.p: Pakistan said on Thursday it had told the United States that neighbour India had created a "dangerous security environment" by deploying medium-range ballistic missiles near their border.
India on Wednesday denied a Washington Post report that it had deployed the Prithvi missiles along any international border.

Foreign Minister Gohar Ayub Khan sent a letter to U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright on Wednesday, saying Pakistan had to take "appropriate counter measures", a Foreign Ministry spokesman said.
"The foreign minister has warned that the Indian action has created a dangerous security environment," the spokesman said.
"The Indian action bears the potential of unleashing a ballistic missile race in South Asia," he quoted Khan's letter as saying.
"The threat posed by this escalatory action would leave us no choice but to take appropriate counter-measures."
The spokesman declined to specify the counter-measures Pakistan could take and said Islamabad would study and evaluate "all these reports" of the deployment and the Indian denial.
Pakistan Army chief General Jehangir Karamat said in a speech on Wednesday that Islamabad must develop an "indigenous capability" to meet the Indian missile threat.

The Foreign Ministry spokesman quoted Khan as telling Albright in the letter that "India appears to have been encouraged by the discriminatory American legislation against Pakistan that has resulted in a serious military imbalance in the region".
This was a reference to the so-called U.S. Pressler Amendment law under which the United States stopped weapons sales to Pakistan in 1990 on suspicion that Islamabad was developing nuclear weapons.
The United States on Tuesday declared itself in "outright opposition" to the deployment of ballistic missiles by India and Pakistan, and said it was working to prevent such moves.
U.S. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns, speaking at a news briefing in Washington, refused to confirm that India had moved such weapons to a prospective launch site.
The Washington Post said U.S. intelligence agencies had concluded that less than a dozen missiles were now located near the city of Jullundur in the state of Punjab in northwest India.
The Prithvi missiles currently are capable of carrying conventional but not nuclear warheads.

There have been repeated reports that Pakistan obtained M-11 missiles from China, which Islamabad denies, but Burns said Washington still had not decided that actual deployment of the Indian missiles had taken place.
Pakistan and India have fought three wars since their independence from Britain in 1947.
